patterns.title: Washington's hold on the IMF and World Bank
patterns.summary:
The United States holds 16.49% of the votes at the IMF, the largest share of any member. Major policy decisions need 85% of the total vote, so a share above 15% lets the US block them alone; day-to-day decisions such as approving a single loan program need only 50% (Congressional Research Service, March 2025). By an informal agreement among members, the World Bank president has always been a US citizen nominated by Washington, and the IMF managing director a European: every IMF head from 1946 to 2019 came from Belgium, Sweden, France, the Netherlands, Germany or Spain, and the current head, Kristalina Georgieva, is Bulgarian. The IMF's number two, the first deputy managing director, has gone to an American under the same arrangement: Stanley Fischer (1994-2001), Anne Krueger (2001-2006), John Lipsky (2006-2011), David Lipton (2011-2020), Geoffrey Okamoto (2020-2022) and Gita Gopinath (from January 2022). Lipton and Okamoto came straight from senior US Treasury posts.

Treasury officials took part directly in some of the largest rescues. In 1995 the Clinton administration lent Mexico up to $20 billion through the Treasury's Exchange Stabilization Fund. In December 1997 Treasury Under Secretary David Lipton flew to Seoul to test whether President-elect Kim Dae-jung would back labour-market reforms before a $10 billion emergency package was announced on 24 December. In 2018 the IMF gave Argentina its largest stand-by arrangement ever, US$57 billion (1,227% of Argentina's quota), with President Trump publicly backing the deal; the IMF's own 2021 evaluation found it did not meet its goals. Statistical studies find that countries closer to Washington get IMF loans more often (Thacker 1999; Barro and Lee 2005), that elected UN Security Council members get more IMF and World Bank programs and about 30% fewer IMF conditions (Dreher, Sturm and Vreeland 2009, 2010), and that World Bank payouts to US-aligned countries depend less on their economic performance (Kilby 2009). Stone (2008) finds US influence narrows conditions only in important, vulnerable countries; elsewhere the IMF acts with broad autonomy.

countries.note: Holds 16.49% of IMF votes, above the 15% needed to block decisions that require 85% (CRS IF10676, March 2025). Nominates every World Bank president, and the IMF's first deputy managing director has been an American since 1994 (Federal Reserve History; IMF press releases).

Five of twelve IMF managing directors were French: Schweitzer (1963-73), de Larosiere (1978-87), Camdessus (1987-2000), Strauss-Kahn (2007-11) and Lagarde (2011-19), per the IMF's list of managing directors.
Horst Kohler, Germany's deputy finance minister 1990-93 and EBRD president from 1998, was IMF managing director from 1 May 2000 to 4 March 2004 (IMF biography).
Rodrigo de Rato, Spain's economy minister under Aznar, was IMF managing director from 7 June 2004 to 31 October 2007 (IMF list; The Local, 2018).
H. Johannes Witteveen was IMF managing director from 1 September 1973 to 16 June 1978 (IMF list).
Camille Gutt, the first IMF managing director, served from 6 May 1946 to 5 May 1951 (IMF list).
Ivar Rooth (1951-56) and Per Jacobsson (1956-63) were the second and third IMF managing directors (IMF list).
Kristalina Georgieva has been IMF managing director since 1 October 2019 (IMF list), keeping the post with a European.

In the 1995 peso crisis the Clinton administration, advised by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, provided $20 billion in loan guarantees from the Exchange Stabilization Fund; Wikipedia reports Treasury made a $580 million profit. Under Secretary Lawrence Summers handled the response (Wikipedia).

On 19 December 1997 Korean envoy Kim Ki-hwan presented an 'IMF Plus' reform package to Deputy Treasury Secretary Summers; on 22 December Treasury Under Secretary David Lipton met President-elect Kim Dae-jung in Seoul and raised labour-market flexibility; on 24 December the IMF and 13 economies announced $10 billion in emergency money (JoongAng Ilbo, 2003).

IMF board approved a stand-by arrangement in June 2018, raised in October 2018 to US$57 billion, 1,227% of quota, the largest in IMF history. Only 4 of 12 reviews were completed, it went off track in August 2019 and was cancelled on 24 July 2020 (IMF PR 21/401). In September 2018 President Trump reaffirmed 'strong U.S. support' for Argentina's IMF engagement (CRS IF10932). Stone (2008) also reports that in 2001 the State Department and National Security Council pushed to extend loans to Argentina while Treasury was at first reluctant.

Stone (2008) cites Russia (1998) among cases where senior US Treasury officials were closely involved in IMF negotiations, and Wikipedia says Deputy Secretary Summers was deeply involved in the Russian crisis response.
Stone (2008) lists Indonesia, with Mexico, Russia and Korea, among programs where senior US Treasury officials were closely involved in negotiations.

Dreher and Vreeland (2011) find that voting with the US on the UN Security Council raises the chance of an IMF program and loan size, but say these results depend largely on Yemen's 1990-91 Council votes.
Stone (2008) names Brazil (1999), with Russia (1998) and Argentina (2001), as programs in which the IMF backed governments defending overvalued exchange rates.

timeline.event: Camille Gutt of Belgium becomes the first IMF managing director, starting an unbroken line of European heads.
Robert McNamara, former US defense secretary, becomes World Bank president; every president since has been a US citizen.
Stanley Fischer becomes the IMF's first deputy managing director, serving until August 2001.
Advised by Treasury Secretary Rubin, the Clinton administration provides $20 billion in loan guarantees to Mexico from the Exchange Stabilization Fund.
On 22 December, Treasury Under Secretary David Lipton meets Korea's president-elect Kim Dae-jung; two days later a $10 billion emergency package is announced.
Thacker finds that countries moving toward the US in UN General Assembly votes are more likely to get IMF loans (87 countries, 1985-1994).
IMF head Horst Kohler proposes American economist Anne Krueger, a former World Bank chief economist, to succeed Fischer as first deputy managing director.
Barro and Lee publish evidence that IMF loans are larger and more frequent for countries with closer political and economic ties to the US and major European countries.
John Lipsky, vice chairman of JPMorgan Investment Bank, becomes IMF first deputy managing director on 1 September.
Stone finds US influence narrows IMF conditions, but only in important, vulnerable countries that receive US aid.
Dreher, Sturm and Vreeland find temporary UN Security Council members are more likely to be in IMF programs (197 countries, 1951-2004) and get more World Bank projects (157 countries, 1970-2004).
Kilby finds World Bank structural adjustment payouts to US-aligned countries depend less on economic performance (97 countries, 1984-2005).
David Lipton, a former Treasury under secretary who later worked at Moore Capital and Citi, becomes IMF first deputy managing director on 1 September.
The IMF approves a stand-by arrangement for Argentina in June, raised in October to US$57 billion, the largest in its history.
In September, President Trump reaffirms strong US support for Argentina's engagement with the IMF.
Treasury Secretary Mnuchin welcomes the proposal to make Treasury's Geoffrey Okamoto the IMF's first deputy managing director.
Argentina cancels the 2018 arrangement on 24 July after only 4 of 12 planned reviews.
The IMF's ex-post evaluation finds the Argentina program did not meet its goals and created substantial financial and reputational risk for the Fund.
Gita Gopinath, a US citizen, replaces Okamoto as first deputy managing director on 21 January.
The Congressional Research Service reports the US holds 16.49% of IMF votes, enough to veto decisions that need 85%.

statistical_studies.study: Strom C. Thacker, 'The High Politics of IMF Lending', World Politics, 1999
statistical_studies.sample: 87 developing countries, 1985-1994, 746 country-years; pooled logit on whether a country got an IMF Stand-By or Extended Fund Facility loan in a year; UN alignment from State Department 'key votes'
statistical_studies.finding: Movement toward the US in UN General Assembly votes is the strongest political predictor of getting a loan (significant at the 1% level; a 0.10 shift raises the log-odds by about 0.29). The level of alignment is weak and loses significance after correcting for autocorrelation; it matters only in 1990-94. The author warns UN votes may proxy for other traits.

statistical_studies.study: Thomas Barnebeck Andersen, Thomas Harr and Finn Tarp, 'On US Politics and IMF Lending', University of Copenhagen Discussion Paper 04-11, 2004
statistical_studies.sample: 68 developing countries, 1986-1994, 558 country-years, re-using Thacker's model
statistical_studies.finding: A measure of 'political payments' toward the US raises loan chances (significant at 5%) and takes over from Thacker's movement variable; the authors call the evidence fairly weak and sensitive to specification.

statistical_studies.study: Robert J. Barro and Jong-Wha Lee, 'IMF Programs: Who Is Chosen and What Are the Effects?', Journal of Monetary Economics, 2005 (NBER Working Paper 8951)
statistical_studies.finding: IMF quota share, share of nationals on IMF staff, and UN voting with the US are positive and at least marginally significant for program participation; for loan size, trade with the US and quota share are significant at 5%, staff share and UN voting with the US at 10%. Voting alignment with France, Germany and the UK also raises participation. Using these as instruments, more IMF lending is followed by lower growth.

statistical_studies.study: Axel Dreher, Jan-Egbert Sturm and James Raymond Vreeland, 'Global horse trading: IMF loans for votes in the United Nations Security Council', European Economic Review 53(7): 742-757, 2009
statistical_studies.finding: Robust positive link between temporary Security Council membership and taking part in IMF programs; membership is also associated with fewer conditions.

statistical_studies.study: Axel Dreher, Jan-Egbert Sturm and James Raymond Vreeland, 'Development aid and international politics: Does membership on the UN Security Council influence World Bank decisions?', Journal of Development Economics 88(1): 1-18, 2009
statistical_studies.finding: Temporary Security Council membership is robustly associated with more World Bank projects; it does not affect the size of World Bank loans.

statistical_studies.study: Axel Dreher, Jan-Egbert Sturm and James Vreeland, 'Does membership on the UN Security Council influence IMF conditionality?', Courant Research Centre Discussion Paper 36, 2010; published as 'Politics and IMF Conditionality', Journal of Conflict Resolution 59(1): 120-148, 2015
statistical_studies.sample: Up to 314 IMF arrangements with 101 countries, 1992-2008 (working paper version)
statistical_studies.finding: Security Council members receive about 30% fewer conditions on IMF loans. Figures are from the 2010 working paper; the 2015 journal text was not opened.

statistical_studies.study: Axel Dreher and Nathan Jensen, 'Independent Actor or Agent? An Empirical Analysis of the Impact of US Interests on IMF Conditions', KOF Working Paper 118, 2005
statistical_studies.sample: 206 IMF letters of intent from 38 countries, 1997-2003
statistical_studies.finding: Countries voting more often with the US in the UN General Assembly get fewer conditions; moving the voting index from 0 to 1 cuts about three conditions, mainly structural benchmarks, not performance criteria.

statistical_studies.study: Christopher Kilby, 'The political economy of conditionality: An empirical analysis of World Bank loan disbursements', Journal of Development Economics 89(1): 51-61, 2009
statistical_studies.finding: Disbursements are less dependent on macroeconomic performance in countries aligned with the US (UN voting), pointing to donor pressure as a cause of weak enforcement.

statistical_studies.study: Randall W. Stone, 'The Scope of IMF Conditionality', International Organization 62(4): 589-620, 2008
statistical_studies.sample: About 96 countries with IMF programs, 1992-2002, IMF MONA conditionality records, by country-month (working paper version)
statistical_studies.finding: US aid is linked to narrower conditions only in vulnerable countries that are important US aid recipients; for high-capacity, highly vulnerable states one standard deviation more US aid cuts conditions by about a third. UN voting similarity with the US has no significant effect. In ordinary cases the IMF has broad autonomy.

statistical_studies.study: Axel Dreher and James Raymond Vreeland, 'Buying Votes and International Organizations', Gottingen Discussion Paper 123, 2011
statistical_studies.finding: Voting with the US on the Security Council is linked to IMF programs (10% level) and larger loans, but the authors say this depends largely on Yemen 1990-91; voting against the US lowers program chances and loan size (5% level) and is not outlier-driven.

uncertain: The studies show statistical links, not orders from Washington. Stone (2008) finds US influence only in important, vulnerable countries and broad IMF autonomy elsewhere; Thacker (1999) finds the level of alignment with the US is not a robust predictor; Andersen, Harr and Tarp (2004) call their own evidence fairly weak.

Current vote shares for every member could not be read from the IMF's own quotas and voting power page (the table did not load); the 16.49% US figure comes from the Congressional Research Service, March 2025.

Whether Washington pressed the IMF to make the 2018 Argentina loan so large is not established here: the IMF's evaluation does not mention the US, and the CRS records only public support from President Trump.

Oatley and Yackee (2004, International Politics 41: 429) is described by a Swiss National Bank summary as linking bank interests to larger IMF programmes and softer conditions; its sample, period and exact finding could not be opened.
The 30% fewer conditions figure comes from the 2010 working paper; the numbers in the 2015 Journal of Conflict Resolution version were not checked.
The Thacker and Barro-Lee findings are about which countries get loans and how large, not how many conditions they carry.

patterns.title: Revolving door: Wall Street, finance ministries, lenders
patterns.summary:
The top jobs at the IMF and World Bank are filled largely by people moving between national finance ministries or central banks, private banks and funds, and back. World Bank presidents Alden Clausen (Bank of America CEO, 1981-86 at the Bank, then back to Bank of America as chairman and CEO), Lewis Preston (J.P. Morgan), Robert Zoellick (Goldman Sachs vice chairman 2006-07; Goldman's chairman of international advisors 2013-16), David Malpass (Bear Stearns chief economist, then Treasury under secretary) and Ajay Banga (Mastercard CEO, General Atlantic) all came from finance. At the IMF, first deputies moved between Treasury, Wall Street and the Fund: Stanley Fischer left the IMF in 2001 and was Citigroup vice chairman from February 2002 to April 2005; John Lipsky came from JPMorgan; David Lipton went from Treasury (1993-98) to Moore Capital and Citi, then to the IMF (2011); Geoffrey Okamoto went straight from acting Treasury under secretary to the IMF in 2020.

European managing directors came from finance ministries and central banks: Michel Camdessus (Banque de France governor 1984-87), Horst Kohler (German deputy finance minister 1990-93, savings banks association, EBRD), Rodrigo de Rato (Spanish economy minister 1996-2004), Christine Lagarde (Baker McKenzie global chairman 1999-2005, French finance minister 2007-11, later ECB president). Two were later convicted: Rato, chairman of Bankia after the IMF, received 4.5 years for misusing company credit cards (upheld by Spain's Supreme Court in October 2018) and a further 4 years 9 months for tax crimes, money laundering and corruption in December 2024; Lagarde was found guilty of negligence by France's Court of Justice of the Republic in December 2016 over a EUR 403 million arbitration award, with no penalty. In Washington, Robert Rubin went from Goldman Sachs co-chairman to Treasury secretary (1995-99) and then Citigroup (1999-2009, about $126 million in pay); Lawrence Summers went from World Bank chief economist to Treasury and later to the hedge fund D. E. Shaw. At the IFC, Goldman Sachs partner Jin-Yong Cai became chief executive in 2012 and joined private equity firm TPG in 2016.

countries.role: Treasury, Wall Street and lender seats
countries.note: Washington hosts the IMF, World Bank, IFC and Treasury; New York hosts Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, JPMorgan and Bear Stearns. Documented moves include Clausen, Rubin, Summers, Fischer, Lipsky, Lipton, Okamoto, Zoellick, Malpass and Banga (sources in timeline).

countries.role: European ministry or central bank to IMF
countries.note: Camdessus was Banque de France governor (Nov 1984-Jan 1987) before heading the IMF (1987-2000); Lagarde was French finance minister (2007-11) before heading the IMF (2011-19) and was found guilty of negligence in 2016 over the Tapie award she sent to arbitration as minister (BNN Bloomberg).

countries.role: European ministry or central bank to IMF
countries.note: Kohler was Germany's deputy finance minister (1990-93) and president of the German Savings Bank Association (1993-98) before the EBRD and the IMF (2000-04). Lagarde moved from the IMF to the European Central Bank in Frankfurt in November 2019 (ECB CV).

countries.role: European ministry or central bank to IMF
countries.note: Rato was economy minister (1996-2004), IMF head (2004-07), then Bankia chairman (2010-12); convicted in 2017 of misusing about EUR 12 million in Caja Madrid and Bankia company cards with 64 others, sentence of 4.5 years confirmed in 2018 (The Local), and sentenced in December 2024 to 4 years 9 months for tax crimes (Gulf News).

Kohler became president of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development in London in September 1998, then left for the IMF in 2000 (IMF biography). Lipsky ran Salomon Brothers' European analysis group in London from 1989 (Wikipedia).
Fischer went from IMF first deputy (1994-2001) to Citigroup vice chairman (2002-05) to Bank of Israel governor (2005-13), then US Federal Reserve vice chairman (2014-17) (Federal Reserve History).

Jin-Yong Cai, a Chinese national who worked at Morgan Stanley, China International Capital Corporation and Goldman Sachs (managing partner), became IFC chief executive in October 2012 (Bretton Woods Project) and joined TPG as a partner from 1 February 2016 (Private Equity Wire).

timeline.event: Bank of America president and CEO Alden Clausen becomes World Bank president on 1 July.
Clausen leaves the World Bank and returns to Bank of America as chairman and CEO.
Banque de France governor Michel Camdessus becomes IMF managing director on 16 January.
Lawrence Summers becomes World Bank chief economist, then moves to Treasury as under secretary for international affairs in 1993.
Robert Rubin, Goldman Sachs co-chairman until 1992, is sworn in as Treasury secretary after a 99-0 Senate vote.
Rubin leaves Treasury and joins Citigroup in October as chairman of the executive committee.
Horst Kohler, former German deputy finance minister and EBRD president, becomes IMF managing director on 1 May.
Stanley Fischer, IMF first deputy until August 2001, becomes Citigroup vice chairman in February.
Rodrigo de Rato, Spain's former economy minister, becomes IMF managing director on 7 June.
JPMorgan's John Lipsky becomes IMF first deputy managing director on 1 September.
Robert Zoellick moves from Goldman Sachs vice chairman to World Bank president on 1 July.
Christine Lagarde, French finance minister and earlier Baker McKenzie global chairman, becomes IMF managing director.
David Lipton, ex-Treasury official who worked at Moore Capital and Citi, becomes IMF first deputy on 1 September.
Goldman Sachs managing partner Jin-Yong Cai becomes chief executive of the IFC in October.
Goldman Sachs names former World Bank president Zoellick chairman of its international advisors.
Cai leaves the IFC to become a partner at private equity firm TPG from 1 February.
France's Court of Justice of the Republic finds Lagarde guilty of negligence over a EUR 403 million award to Bernard Tapie, with no penalty.
Spain's Supreme Court confirms Rato's 4.5-year sentence for misusing Caja Madrid and Bankia company cards.
David Malpass, former Bear Stearns chief economist and Treasury under secretary, becomes World Bank president on 9 April.
Acting Treasury under secretary Geoffrey Okamoto moves directly to IMF first deputy managing director.
Ajay Banga, former Mastercard CEO and General Atlantic vice chairman, becomes World Bank president on 2 June.
A Madrid court sentences Rato to 4 years 9 months for tax crimes, money laundering and corruption; he says he will appeal.

uncertain: A career move between a lender and a bank is not proof that any loan decision favoured that bank; no source opened here ties a specific IMF or World Bank decision to a later private job.

The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission referred Rubin for possibly violating US law in his Citigroup role, but the Justice Department did not pursue it (as reported on Wikipedia; the FCIC referral itself was not opened).
Rato's 2024 tax-crimes conviction was under appeal when reported; the separate case over Bankia's 2011 share listing is not resolved by any source opened here.
Lagarde's 2016 verdict carried no penalty and no criminal record; the IMF board said it would meet to consider the ruling.
Dates for Lipton's years at Moore Capital and Citi, Malpass's years at Bear Stearns and Treasury, and Banga's years at Mastercard are not given in the sources consulted.
